message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a tenant in Texas. (This is general information and not legal advice; for specific situations you may want to consult an attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.) | Category | What You’re Entitled To | How to Exercise It | |----------|------------------------|--------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • The landlord may charge a maximum of **one month’s rent** for a furnished unit and **two months’ rent** for an unfurnished unit.
• The deposit must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Keep a written move‑in inspection report.
• Request a written itemized statement of deductions if the landlord keeps any portion. | | **Habitability** | • The landlord must keep the premises in a safe, sanitary condition (e.g., plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity).
• Repairs must be made within a reasonable time after notice. | • Provide written notice (email or letter) of needed repairs.
• If the landlord fails to act, you may contact the local health or building department, or file a complaint with the Texas Attorney General’s Office. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • You have the right to live without unreasonable interference from the landlord or other tenants. | • Report any harassment or unlawful entry to the landlord in writing. | | **Entry by Landlord** | • Landlord must give **at least 24 hours’ written notice** before entering, except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of all entries; if the landlord enters without notice, you can refuse entry. | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease; late fees are allowed only if stated in the lease. | • Pay rent on time; keep receipts or bank records. | | **Lease Termination** | • For month‑to‑month leases, either party may terminate with **30 days’ written notice**.
• For fixed‑term leases, the landlord may terminate early only for a breach by you or if the lease allows it. | • Provide written notice; keep copies. | | **Discrimination** | • Texas law (and federal Fair Housing Act) prohibits discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income. | • File a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). | | **Repair and Deduct / Rent Withholding** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major defect, you may (1) pay the repair yourself and deduct the cost from rent, or (2) withhold rent until the repair is made. | • Document the defect, notify the landlord in writing, keep receipts, and follow the proper procedure outlined in Texas Property Code §92.001. | | **Eviction Process** | • The landlord must serve a **30‑day notice** for non‑payment of rent or a **60‑day notice** for lease violations.
• After the notice period, the landlord must file an eviction action in court. | • Respond to the notice; attend the court hearing; you may contest the eviction if you have evidence of a lease violation or improper notice. | | **Privacy** | • Landlord cannot enter your unit without notice, except in emergencies. | • Keep a record of any unauthorized entries. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify who pays utilities. If the landlord pays, they must maintain the service. | • Verify utility accounts and keep records of payments. | | **Subletting / Assignment** | • Many leases allow subletting or assignment with landlord’s consent. | • Obtain written permission; keep a copy. | | **Maintenance of Common Areas** | • Landlord must keep common areas clean and safe. | • Report issues in writing; keep a log. | | **Legal Remedies** | • You can sue for damages, recover unpaid rent, or seek injunctive relief if the landlord breaches the lease. | • Consult an attorney; consider small‑claims court for amounts under $10,000. | ### Quick Steps If You Encounter Problems 1. **Document Everything** – Photos, videos, written notices, emails, and receipts. 2. **Notify the Landlord in Writing** – Send a certified mail or email with a read receipt. 3. **Contact Local Authorities** – For habitability issues, call your city’s building or health department. 4. **Seek Legal Aid** – Many Texas cities have free or low‑cost tenant‑rights clinics. 5. **File a Complaint** – If discrimination or unlawful eviction occurs, file with the Texas Commission on Human Rights or HUD. ### Useful Resources | Resource | What It Offers | |----------|----------------| | **Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection** | Information on security deposits, lease disputes, and consumer rights. | | **Texas Commission on Human Rights** | Handles discrimination complaints. | | **HUD – Fair Housing** | National fair housing resources and complaint filing. | | **Local Tenant‑Rights Clinics** | Free legal advice and representation. | | **Texas Property Code** | The statutory law governing landlord‑tenant relationships. | --- **Bottom line:** As a Texas tenant, you have the right to a safe, habitable home, timely repairs, privacy, and protection against discrimination. If a landlord violates these rights, you have several avenues for recourse, from written notices to legal action. If you’re facing a specific issue, let me know the details, and I can help you draft a notice or outline the next steps.
